answer: A way technology has profoundly changed our lives is in how we communicate with one another. The rise of smartphones and social media has made staying in touch almost [[instantaneous]], regardless of distance. This happened incredibly quickly; within about a decade, cheap smartphones and mobile internet reached almost every corner of Bangladesh, even villages like my grandparents'. In the past, keeping in contact with faraway friends and family relied on letters or expensive phone calls, which now seems almost unimaginable. My father still remembers queuing at a shop in town to make a short, crackly call to a relative in Dhaka, and letters took over a week to arrive. Today, a video call across continents is effortless and free, which is genuinely [[remarkable]]. I speak to my elder sister in Dhaka almost every day, and my nephew loves showing me his toys on the screen. On the whole, I think this change has been overwhelmingly positive, keeping relationships alive that might otherwise have faded. However, I do have some [[reservations]]; I feel it has sometimes replaced deeper, face-to-face interaction with shallower digital contact. There is a certain irony that we are more connected than ever yet arguably lonelier. At family gatherings, I sometimes notice everyone staring at their phones instead of talking to the people sitting right next to them. Honestly, like most technology, I think it is a [[double-edged sword]]. Used mindfully, it is an incredible tool, but it requires a degree of [[discipline]]. Overall, though, I am grateful for how it has shrunk the world and brought distant people closer.

followUps.q: Do your grandparents use video calls?
followUps.answer: My grandfather does, surprisingly well for someone in his eighties. My grandmother prefers ordinary calls, because she finds it strange to see her own face on the screen, which always makes us laugh.

followUps.q: Do you still write letters or cards?
followUps.answer: Almost never, sadly. I do sometimes write a card for Eid or a birthday, and people seem to [[treasure]] them far more than a message, precisely because they are so rare now.
